input: Research dual enrollment options for my high schooler

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Dual enrollment can mean community college courses, online programs, AP/IB alternatives, or university partnerships — knowing which types to include or exclude shapes where to look and what to compare.
The student's current grade level, GPA, and academic interests determine which programs they are eligible for and which are worth prioritizing.
The state and school district heavily influence which programs are available, funded, and how credits transfer — some states have universal access laws, others do not.
Cost varies widely — some dual enrollment is tuition-free through the high school, others require out-of-pocket payment — so budget is a hard filter on options.
Whether the student will take classes on a college campus, at their high school, or fully online changes which programs are physically feasible and what the schedule impact is.

The goal could be saving money on future tuition, getting a head start on a specific major, boosting a college application, or academic enrichment — each goal points to different program qualities to prioritize.
Some families want a specific subject area (STEM, humanities, career/technical), which narrows the search considerably and affects which colleges or programs are most relevant.

gold.taskTitle: Research dual enrollment options for your high schooler
gold.taskDescription: Find and evaluate dual enrollment programs that allow the user's high school student to earn college credits while still in high school.

questions.title: What state and school district is your student in?
questions.description: The geographic location determines which programs are legally available, state-funded, and how credits transfer to in-state universities.

questions.title: What grade is your student currently in?
questions.description: Grade level (and GPA if known) affects eligibility requirements for most dual enrollment programs, which often have minimum thresholds.

questions.title: What is the primary goal behind pursuing dual enrollment?
questions.description: Understanding whether the priority is saving on future tuition, enrichment, college application strength, or exploring a career path determines which program qualities matter most.

questions.title: Is there a budget limit, or must options be tuition-free?
questions.description: Some dual enrollment programs are fully funded by the state or school district; others require families to pay. This is a hard filter on which programs are viable.

questions.title: Should classes be on a college campus, at school, or online?
questions.description: The preferred or feasible delivery format — in-person at a college, taught at the high school, or fully online — determines which programs are logistically possible.

questions.title: Are there specific subjects or fields your student wants to focus on?
questions.description: A preference for STEM, humanities, business, healthcare, or career/technical education significantly narrows the search to relevant programs and institutions.

questions.title: Should this research include non-college-credit options like AP or IB?
questions.description: Clarifying whether the scope is strictly dual enrollment (transferable college credits) or also includes AP, IB, and similar accelerated programs changes how broadly to cast the research.
